title: {{NAME}} and the Field Where Magic Grows
moral: Playing your best means playing with your whole heart, not just your feet.

pages.content: The Shimmer Pitch existed only at twilight, when the last stripe of sun fell below the hills and the sky turned the precise colour of a ripe plum. It appeared in the meadow behind the old millhouse, its lines glowing faintly silver, its grass the deep, particular green of a place that is loved and tended by something extraordinary. {{NAME}} had found it three evenings ago, entirely by accident, following a runaway ball. Tonight he came on purpose. The animals were already warming up: a heron named Joss who played with balletic precision on legs like stilts, a pair of identical hedgehog twins called Moss and Midge who specialised in an impenetrable defensive wall, and a retired greyhound named Percy who claimed his best days were behind him but who could still read the game better than anyone on the pitch. The unicorn, whose name was Sylvan and who also happened to be the referee, trotted to the centre circle and planted her hooves with an authority that made the whole meadow feel official.

pages.content: Sylvan had a way of watching that made every player feel simultaneously seen and slightly embarrassed. She stood at the centre spot with her opal horn catching the last threads of light, and she looked at {{NAME}} with enormous violet eyes that seemed to weigh not his skill but something deeper. 'You play well,' she said. 'But you play as if someone is watching and judging.' {{NAME}} felt heat rise to his face. He did play that way, sometimes. The same thought he had on every pitch, an audience in his head, counting his mistakes. 'This pitch is for playing,' said Sylvan. 'Not for performing. There is a difference.' Percy the greyhound ambled over and dropped the ball at {{NAME}}'s feet. 'She said that to me for the first six months,' the greyhound remarked. 'I spent those months waiting to be told off.' He scratched an ear thoughtfully. 'Then I scored the most extraordinary goal of my life, and I don't remember it at all because I was too busy just playing.' {{NAME}} looked down at the ball. Sylvan watched him, patient as a tree.

pages.content: The match was Shimmer Rules, which meant the pitch itself sometimes moved, a left flank becoming a slight hill, a corner becoming a hollow, shifting every fifteen minutes to keep everyone thinking. {{NAME}} had found it maddening in his first game. Tonight it felt like the pitch was teaching him. He stopped watching the imaginary audience in his head. He watched Joss instead, the heron's long neck swinging like a compass needle as he turned, always indicating where he was about to pass. He watched Moss and Midge, who communicated entirely in small grunts, but whose grunts had a pattern as clear as morse code once you listened properly. The first time {{NAME}} anticipated a pass and was already running when the ball left Joss's foot, Percy made a sound that might have been a bark of delight. The pitch shifted beneath them, the right flank tipping into a gentle slope, and {{NAME}} used the slope to curl a shot from an angle that no flat pitch would have allowed, the ball bending in a long, sweet arc into the top corner.

pages.content: When the ball hit the net, Sylvan did something {{NAME}} had never seen a unicorn do. She reared up on her hind legs, her opal horn blazing white, and from the ground where her front hooves landed, a ring of silver flowers bloomed instantly in the grass, spreading outward like ripples in still water. The whole meadow smelled suddenly of rain and honeysuckle. Every player stopped. Even the wind seemed to pause. Joss stood on one leg with an expression of absolute serenity. The hedgehog twins sat down in the silver flowers and began to eat dandelions, apparently considering the moment well served. Percy sat beside {{NAME}} and said nothing at all, which was more eloquent than anything he could have spoken. {{NAME}} felt something loosen in his chest, something that had been tight for a long time, perhaps since the very first pitch he had ever stood on, wondering if he was good enough. Standing in the blooming silver ring, he stopped wondering.

pages.content: The Shimmer Pitch faded when the last light left the sky, its silver lines dissolving slowly like sugar in warm water. {{NAME}} sat in the darkening meadow as the animals dispersed, Percy trotting off into the long grass with a wave of his elegant tail. Joss lifted silently into the sky, a dark, graceful shape against the first stars. The hedgehog twins waddled away shoulder to shoulder, still grunting at each other in their private code. Sylvan was the last to go. She stood before {{NAME}} and pressed her luminous nose gently to his forehead, warm as a small sun. 'Tuesday,' she said simply. He nodded. He tucked his cleats under his arm and walked back across the meadow in the dark, and with each step the grass released a faint silver glow beneath his feet, as if the pitch remembered him. He was almost at the gate when he noticed, attached to the toe of his left cleat, a single silver flower. He slipped it into his pocket and smiled. Tuesday felt a very long way away.
